card.title: COASTWATCHERS
card.text: Your weather cards cost you 1 less. Deployment: Forecast.
card.flavorText: The Coastwatchers were Allied intelligence operatives stationed on remote Pacific islands during WWII. Many were Australians, New Zealanders and Pacific Islanders citizens, with various jobs such as planters, traders, missionaries, and local police. Their task was not to seek battle, but to watch quietly, report Japanese ship and aircraft movements, and help rescue stranded Allied personnel. Lieutenant Commander Eric Feldt led the Australian coastwatching organization for much of the war and gave it the code name Ferdinand, a reference to Ferdinand the Bull, as a reminder that coastwatchers were meant to stay hidden and gather information, not draw attention. Their reports were especially valuable during the Guadalcanal campaign. Hidden observers in the Solomon Islands warned Allied forces about Japanese warships, aircraft, and troop movements. In November 1942, coastwatchers Jack Read and Paul Mason, based on Bougainville, sent early warnings of Japanese movements toward US forces in the Solomons. Admiral William Halsey later credited the coastwatchers with helping save Guadalcanal. Coastwatchers also guided rescues. After PT 109 was sunk, Australian coastwatcher Arthur Evans sent Solomon Islander scouts Biuku Gasa and Eroni Kumana to find the survivors, helping rescue future US president John F. Kennedy and his crew.
